prompt: A regular polygon $P$ has four more sides than another regular polygon $Q$, and their interior angles differ by $1^\circ$. How many sides does $P$ have?

solutions.title: Exterior angles
solutions.body:
Let $P$ have $n$ sides, so $Q$ has $n-4$. Interior angles differ by $1^\circ$, so exterior angles differ by $1^\circ$ too, and $Q$ (fewer sides) has the larger exterior angle:
$$\frac{360}{n-4}-\frac{360}{n}=1 .$$
Multiplying by $n(n-4)$: $360n-360(n-4)=n(n-4)$, i.e. $n^2-4n-1440=0$, i.e. $(n-40)(n+36)=0$. So $n=40$ (and $Q$ has $36$ sides: exterior angles $9^\circ$ and $10^\circ$).

**Answer: $40$**

prompt:
Hudson labels each of the four vertices of a triangular pyramid with a different integer chosen from $1$ to $15$. For each of the four triangular faces, he then calculates the mean of the three numbers at the vertices of the face.

Given that the means calculated by Hudson are all integers, how many different sets of four numbers could he have chosen to label the vertices of the triangular pyramid?

solutions.title: All four numbers are congruent mod $3$
solutions.body:
Let the labels be $a,b,c,d$. The four face sums $a+b+c,\ a+b+d,\ a+c+d,\ b+c+d$ must all be multiples of $3$.

Subtracting two face sums gives the difference of two labels, e.g. $(a+b+c)-(a+b+d)=c-d$. So any two labels are congruent mod $3$: all four labels have the same remainder $r$ mod $3$. Conversely, if they do, every face sum is $\equiv3r\equiv0\pmod3$.

So we need four distinct numbers from $1..15$ with the same remainder mod $3$. Each remainder class has exactly $5$ members ($\{1,4,7,10,13\}$, $\{2,5,8,11,14\}$, $\{3,6,9,12,15\}$), and there are $\binom54=5$ ways to pick four from each class:
$$3\times5=15 .$$

**Answer: $15$**

prompt:
It is possible to write $15129=123^2$ as the sum of three distinct squares: $15129=27^2+72^2+96^2$.

(i) By using the identity $(a+b)^2\equiv a^2+2ab+b^2$, or otherwise, find another way to write $15129$ as the sum of three distinct squares.

(ii) Hence, or otherwise, show that $378225=615^2$ can be written as the sum of six distinct squares.

Mr Evans has a class containing an even number of students. He calculated that in the end-of-term examination the mean mark of the students was $58$, the median mark was $80$ and the difference between the lowest mark and the highest mark was $40$. Show that Mr Evans made a mistake in his calculations.
answer: The marks would have to total at least $120N+40>116N=58\cdot2N$.

solutions.title: Lower bound for the total
solutions.body:
Let there be $2N$ students with marks $a_1\le a_2\le\dots\le a_{2N}$. The given data say
$$\sum a_i=2N\cdot58=116N,\qquad a_N+a_{N+1}=160,\qquad a_{2N}-a_1=40 .$$
Since $a_N\le a_{N+1}$ and they average $80$, $a_{N+1}\ge80$, hence $a_j\ge80$ for all $j\ge N+1$. In particular $a_{2N}\ge80$, so $a_1=a_{2N}-40\ge40$ and every mark is at least $40$.

Therefore
$$\sum a_i=\underbrace{a_1+\dots+a_{N-1}}_{\ge40(N-1)}+\underbrace{(a_N+a_{N+1})}_{160}+\underbrace{a_{N+2}+\dots+a_{2N}}_{\ge80(N-1)}\ \ge\ 120N+40 .$$
But $120N+40>116N$, contradicting $\sum a_i=116N$. So the three statistics cannot all hold: Mr Evans made a mistake. ∎

prompt: A square $ABCD$ has side-length $2$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. The circle $S$ inside the quadrilateral $AMCD$ touches the three sides $AM$, $CD$ and $DA$. What is its radius?

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(2,0)$, $C=(2,2)$, $D=(0,2)$, $M=(2,1)$. A circle of radius $r$ tangent to $DA$ ($x=0$) and $CD$ ($y=2$) and inside the square has centre $(r,\,2-r)$.

The line $AM$ is $y=\tfrac x2$, i.e. $x-2y=0$. The centre lies on the same side as $D$ (where $x-2y<0$), so its distance to $AM$ is
$$\frac{2(2-r)-r}{\sqrt5}=\frac{4-3r}{\sqrt5}.$$
Tangency means this equals $r$: $4-3r=\sqrt5\,r$, so
$$r=\frac4{3+\sqrt5}=\frac{4(3-\sqrt5)}{9-5}=3-\sqrt5\approx0.764 .$$

**Answer: $3-\sqrt5$**

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body: Let $O$ be the centre and $r$ the radius. The perpendicular to $AB$ through $O$ meets $AB$ at $P$, $AM$ at $Q$ and $CD$ at $U$; then $PU=2$ and $AP=r$, $OU=r$. Triangle $AQP$ is similar to $AMB$ (as $PQ\parallel BM$), so $PQ=\tfrac12AP=\tfrac r2$. If $T$ is the point of tangency on $AM$, triangle $OQT$ is similar to $AMB$ too ($\angle OTQ=90^\circ$, $\angle OQT=\angle AMB$), so $OQ=OT\cdot\dfrac{AM}{AB}=\dfrac{\sqrt5}2r$. Then $2=PQ+QO+OU=\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt5}2+1\right)r$, so $r=\dfrac4{3+\sqrt5}=3-\sqrt5$.

prompt:
A robot sits at zero on a number line. Each second the robot chooses a direction, left or right, and at the $s$th second the robot moves $2^{s-1}$ units in that direction on the number line.

For which integers $n$ are there infinitely many routes the robot can take to reach $n$?

(You may use the fact that every positive integer can be written as a sum of different powers of $2$. For example, $19=2^0+2^1+2^4$.)
answer: Exactly the odd integers (positive or negative).

solutions.title: Parity, and counting routes of each length
solutions.body:
A route of length $t$ ends at $\varepsilon_1\cdot1+\varepsilon_2\cdot2+\dots+\varepsilon_t2^{t-1}$ with each $\varepsilon_i=\pm1$.

**Even $n$ are impossible.** The first move is $\pm1$ (odd) and every later move is even, so the robot is always at an odd position.

**Every odd $n$ is reached by infinitely many routes.** Fix $t$. Let $T=\{i:\varepsilon_i=+1\}$ and $S=\sum_{i\in T}2^{i-1}$, so $S$ is an integer in $[0,2^t-1]$ and every such integer $S$ arises from exactly one choice of signs (binary expansion: this is the quoted fact). The final position is
$$\sum_{i\in T}2^{i-1}-\sum_{i\notin T}2^{i-1}=2S-(2^t-1).$$
As $S$ runs through $0,1,\dots,2^t-1$ this takes **every odd value from $-(2^t-1)$ to $2^t-1$, exactly once**.

Now let $n$ be odd. For every $t$ with $2^t-1\ge|n|$ there is a route of length $t$ ending at $n$ (take $S=\frac{n+2^t-1}2$). Routes of different lengths are different, and there are infinitely many such $t$. So odd $n$ have infinitely many routes.

**Answer: exactly the odd integers.** ∎
